title: Checks, captures, threats: look at the forcing moves first (part 1 of 3)

steps.caption: White to move. Nothing is explained yet. White has two checks. Which would you try first?

claims.statement: The check on h7 loses the queen.

steps.prompt: Before you read on: what is the first thing you looked at, and why?

line.say: The knight gives check. Black must deal with the check before anything else.
The queen takes on h7 with check, and the king has nowhere to go: checkmate.

claims.statement: Nf6+ forces checkmate in two.

steps.text: **Forcing moves** leave the opponent very few choices. There are three kinds. A **check** attacks the king. A **capture** takes a piece. A **threat** is a quiet move that will win something, or mate, if ignored. The habit this lesson builds: list these first, look at every reply, then decide. It is where to look first, not proof that one of them works.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight can check from e2. Step through the idea.

line.say: The knight checks the king, and nothing of White's can capture it.
The rook checks along the fourth rank. The king has no safe square: checkmate.

claims.statement: Ne2+ forces checkmate in two.
No white piece attacks the knight on e2.

steps.caption: White to move. White has three checks with the queen: to g6, h7 or g3. Only one of them is good.

claims.statement: The check on g3 forces mate in two.
The check on h7 loses the queen.
The check on g6 loses the queen.

steps.caption: Now the good check, step by step.

line.say: Check along the g-file. No black piece can take the queen on g3.
The queen lands on g7, guarded by the bishop on h6. The king cannot take it: checkmate.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks the queen on g3.
Qg3+ forces checkmate in two.

steps.caption: White to move. A capture: the bishop on e2 attacks the black bishop on g4, and the queen stands behind it on the same diagonal.

line.say: The queen, which waited behind the bishop, takes the knight. White has won a piece.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks g4 directly.
One black piece defends g4.
Bxg4 wins a piece along the engine line.

steps.caption: White to move. No check, and no capture wins anything. A quiet pawn move makes a threat.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen on d7 and the rook on b7 at the same time.
The queen moves away; the rook is still attacked.
Black takes the pawn back. White has won a rook for a pawn.

claims.statement: After the push, the pawn attacks d7.
After the push, the pawn attacks b7.
The push wins material along the engine line.

steps.text: Why list them first? Because they **shrink the tree**. In 7,465 positions with the side to move in check (1,500 Lichess games, January 2013), the mean was 3.3 legal replies, and 86% had five or fewer [V]. In 88,464 positions with no check, the mean was 31.5 [V]. A capture usually invites one recapture [I]. [H] Naming the three kinds may also make an opponent's check or capture harder to miss.

steps.caption: White's queen has just checked from b3. Count Black's legal replies. A check can leave very few.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly one legal move.

line.say: Only Be6 blocks the check, and the king has no square. One legal reply.

steps.caption: Another position after a check. Now Black has four replies, of three kinds: take the checker, block, or move the king. Which is which?

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly four legal moves.

steps.caption: The three kinds of answer. The queen can take the checker. The queen or the f-pawn can block on f5. The king can step to b8.

claims.statement: Black's four legal replies are the three kinds.

steps.text: Three kinds of answer to a check: **take** the checker, **block** between the checker and the king, or **move** the king. A knight check cannot be blocked. Sorting the replies this way makes a check easy to read to the end.

Counts from Lichess games (January 2013), recalled from an earlier run that cannot be reproduced now [R]: the best move was quiet about 70% of the time, a capture about 20 to 25%, and a check 5 to 10%, depending on how a capture with a check is counted. A reviewer's recount of 18,420 Lichess puzzles [S] found 62% begin with a check. [I] Forcing moves are where tactics hide, not where most moves are.

steps.caption: White to move. List the checks and captures. Do any of them win material?

claims.statement: No line wins more than a pawn for White.
The engine rates the position as roughly level.

steps.text: No check exists here, and no capture wins anything. Saying so is a result, not a failure: you looked, and you can move on to quiet moves.

steps.title: Same check, one change
steps.prompt: The first position is a forced win by a check. In the second, the rook has moved. In the third, a pawn far away has moved. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **Remember.** Before you decide, list the forcing moves: checks, captures and threats. They leave the opponent few replies, so they are quick to read to the end. A check can be answered by taking the checker, blocking, or moving the king. Forcing is not the same as good, so look at every reply, and if nothing works, say so and move on.
